paragraphs: A further advantage resulted from this custom. The citizens from the country had time, between the two elections, to inform themselves about the merits of the candidate who had been provisionally nominated, and did not have to vote without knowing the case. But under the pretext of hastening matters, this custom was abolished, and both elections were held on the same day.

The _Comitia Tributa_ were properly the council of the Roman people. They were convoked by the tribunes alone. At them the tribunes were elected and passed their plebiscita. The senate not only had no standing in them but had no right even to be present. The senators, forced to obey laws on which they could not vote, were in this respect less free than the humblest citizens. This injustice was altogether ill-conceived, and was enough by itself to invalidate the decrees of a body to which not all its members were admitted. Had all the patricians attended the comitia by virtue of their right as citizens, they would not, as mere private individuals, have had any considerable influence on a vote counted by heads, where the humblest proletarian was as good as the _princeps senatus_.

It may be seen, therefore, that besides the order achieved by these various ways of distributing so great a people and taking its votes, the various methods were not forms indifferent in themselves. The results of each depended on the aims for which it was preferred.

Without going into further details here, we may gather from what has been said that the _Comitia Tributa_ were the most favorable to popular government, and the _Comitia Centuriata_ to aristocracy. The _Comitia Curiata_, in which the common people of Rome formed the majority, were fitted only to further tyranny and evil designs. They naturally fell into disrepute, and even seditious persons avoided a method that revealed their plans too clearly. It is beyond dispute that the whole majesty of the Roman people lay solely in the _Comitia Centuriata_, which alone included everyone. For the _Comitia Curiata_ excluded the rural tribes, and the _Comitia Tributa_ excluded the senate and the patricians.

As for the method of taking the vote, among the ancient Romans it was as simple as their morals, although not so simple as at Sparta. Each man declared his vote aloud, and a clerk duly wrote it down. The majority in each tribe determined the vote of the tribe, the majority of the tribes that of the people, and so with the _curiæ_ and centuries. This custom was good as long as honesty prevailed among the citizens and each man was ashamed to vote publicly for an unjust proposal or an unworthy candidate. But when the people grew corrupt and votes were bought, it was fitting that voting be secret, so that buyers would be held back by mistrust, and rogues be given a means of not being traitors.

I know that Cicero attacks this change and blames it in part for the ruin of the Republic. But though I feel the weight that Cicero’s authority must carry on such a point, I cannot agree with him. I hold, on the contrary, that for want of enough such changes the destruction of the State is bound to be hastened. Just as a regimen of health does not suit the sick, we should not try to govern a corrupted people by the laws that a good people requires. There is no better proof of this rule than the long life of the Republic of Venice, of which the shadow still exists, solely because its laws are suited only to wicked men.

The citizens were therefore given tablets by means of which each man could vote without anyone knowing how he voted. New methods were also introduced for collecting the tablets, for counting voices, for comparing numbers, and so on. But all these precautions did not prevent the good faith of the officers charged with these functions[2] from often being suspected. Finally, to prevent intrigues and trafficking in votes, edicts were issued, but their very number proves how useless they were.

Toward the close of the Republic, it was often necessary to resort to extraordinary expedients to make up for the inadequacy of the laws. Sometimes miracles were pretended. This method might deceive the people, but it could not deceive those who governed. Sometimes an assembly was hastily called together before the candidates had time to form their factions. Sometimes a whole sitting was taken up with talk, when it was seen that the people had been won over and was on the point of taking the wrong side. But in the end ambition eluded every attempt to check it. And the most incredible fact of all is that, in the midst of all these abuses, the vast people, thanks to its ancient regulations, never ceased to elect magistrates, to pass laws, to judge cases, and to carry on business both public and private, almost as easily as the senate itself could have done.
